request.question: Why does gradient descent move opposite to the gradient?

response.answer:
Gradient descent moves opposite to the gradient because this direction reduces the value of the objective function. The gradient, \(\nabla_\theta J(\theta)\), points in the direction of the steepest ascent of the objective function \(J(\theta)\). By moving in the opposite direction, the algorithm ensures that the parameters \(\theta\) are updated to minimize \(J(\theta)\). This is captured in the formula \(\theta := \theta - \alpha \nabla_\theta J(\theta)\), where \(\alpha > 0\) is the learning rate that controls the step size.

This explanation is supported by the evidence from **Gradient Descent (lec_02) 0-35s**, where it is stated: "Move parameters opposite to the gradient to reduce the objective," and the formula \(\theta := \theta - \alpha \nabla_\theta J(\theta)\) is shown.

For further clarification, refer to **Gradient Descent (lec_02) 0-35s**.
